h1: Coming back to brew in India after training overseas
title: Brewing in India After Training Abroad | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when you bring overseas brewing training back to India: raw materials, water, heat, kit size, excise paperwork and team training.
teaser: Your training was solid. Then you meet a borewell, a 40 °C May and a malt delivery that sat in a truck for a week.
standfirst: Brewers who train in Germany, the UK, the US or Australia come home with good habits. Some of those habits need adjusting for Indian conditions. Here is what usually changes and how to adapt without losing your standards.
sections:
A good overseas programme teaches process thinking, hygiene, sensory discipline and respect for numbers. None of that stops being true in India. What changes are the conditions around the brewery and the way the business runs.

Brewers who struggle after coming back are rarely short of knowledge. They are usually trying to run an Indian brewpub exactly like the training brewery they left, with the same assumptions about raw materials, water and staff. The ones who settle quickly treat their first months as a recalibration. Our guide to brewing for India covers the climate side in detail.

Most specialty malt and nearly all aroma hops in Indian craft brewing are imported. They spend weeks in shipping and may sit in warm warehouses before reaching you. Check the date and the storage history of every delivery. Hops should arrive cold and vacuum packed. They should go straight into a freezer or cold room.

Malt picks up moisture in the monsoon. A sack that has absorbed water mills differently and can lose extract, so watch your brewhouse efficiency when the weather turns. Indian base malt and adjuncts such as rice and maize are widely used in mainstream lager. Some brewpubs use them too. If your training was all malt, spend time learning how adjunct mashes behave.

In many training breweries the water report arrives once a year and barely changes. In India the source can change with the season. Borewell water is often hard and high in bicarbonate. Municipal supply may carry chlorine or chloramine. Some brewpubs switch between sources or tankers without telling the brewer.

Test your water regularly, not once. Many Indian brewpubs use reverse osmosis and build their water back up with brewing salts, which gives control if the RO plant is maintained. Carbon filtration for chlorine is not optional, because chlorophenols survive into finished beer and taste medicinal.

Ambient temperatures above 35 °C for months put pressure on everything. Glycol chillers work harder. Wort cooling takes longer if your incoming water is warm, which can push you to use a two stage heat exchanger or chilled water. Yeast stored without proper refrigeration loses viability fast.

The cold chain after the brewery is the part overseas brewers underestimate most. A keg that leaves your cold room at 2 °C may sit in a warm van or a hot back room before it reaches the tap. You will need to talk to the bar and logistics teams about this more than you ever did abroad.

Many Indian brewpubs run a 5 to 10 hectolitre brewhouse with a small team. As head brewer you may also be the maintenance person, the purchaser and the trainer. Pumps, seals and chillers fail. Spare parts can take time to arrive, so a basic spares stock and a relationship with a local fabricator matter.

You will also deal with excise. Brewpubs keep registers of production, stock and sales. State rules differ on what must be recorded and when. Ask the owner or the licensing adviser what is expected and keep your records exact from day one. Rules vary by state and change, so check the current notification rather than relying on what a previous brewer did.

Your assistants may have learned on the job from someone with different habits. Some will be excellent. Some will have picked up shortcuts. Avoid arriving with a list of everything wrong. Pick the two or three changes that matter most for beer quality, usually cleaning, oxygen control and fermentation temperature. Fix those first.

Write things down. A short standard procedure for brew day and cleaning, in the language your team is most comfortable with, does more than repeated corrections. Teaching the basics clearly is a skill of its own. Having a shared foundation course for your assistants saves you explaining the same thing many times.

1. Test the water at every source and record it.
  2. Check malt and hop storage, dates and condition.
  3. Calibrate thermometers, pH meters and hydrometers.
  4. Walk the cold chain from cold room to tap.
  5. Read the excise registers and ask how they are kept.
  6. Write brew day and cleaning procedures with the team.
  7. Taste every beer on tap with fresh eyes and note the faults.

Do this before changing any recipe. The recipe is rarely the first problem.
faqs: Will an overseas brewing qualification help me get a job in India?
It usually helps, especially for head brewer roles. Employers will still want to see that you can handle local raw materials, water and equipment.
What is the biggest adjustment for brewers returning to India?
Usually heat and the cold chain, followed by variable water. Both affect beer quality more than recipe choices.
Do I need to learn excise rules myself?
You need to understand the records you are responsible for. Work with the owner and a licensing adviser for the detail, because rules vary by state and change.
